content:
I woke with Mio standing in the corner.

Not as a voice. Not as pressure at the back of my thoughts, or some private comment I could pretend no one else had heard. She was just there, looking around the room as if she expected it to have hidden teeth.

The safehouse bedroom had always been ugly: cheap rental carpet, a suspicious beige ceiling, a broken lamp. Dust, instant coffee, and cheap disinfectant made up its whole atmosphere. I’d been able to treat all of that as a private kind of wrongness. Now there was a person in the corner, and the layer between strange and the rest of the world was gone.

“Why are you staring?” she asked.

“I’m trying to see if you disappear when I blink.”

“Rude way to wake up.”

I blinked anyway. She remained.

I reached for the blanket. My hand passed straight through her knee.

Mio flinched. “Warn me before you do that.”

“I didn’t mean to.”

“That’s what makes it worse.”

I pulled my hand back. My face felt hot. “Can you feel anything?”

She watched me carefully. “That’s a broad question.”

“Physically. Or emotionally.”

She gave me a look like I was acting like someone who understood her too well.

“That was always the case,” she said.

The practical questions came back in pieces. The limiter was stable—for the moment. The projection wasn’t. I had no idea how long she’d stay visible, or exactly what the limits were. But she seemed more alive like this than she had when she was only audible. I could see her shoulders tighten; the breath she took before answering; the way she decided where to put her hands.

I could see her fear now.

Mio started pacing the narrow strip of floor between the futon and the kitchenette counter. She moved with a slight lag, as if her body and the room hadn’t quite agreed on the same timing. I kept glancing toward her. My body had already decided she was the center of the room.

Then I realized she was watching me, too.

The door opened. Nico appeared in the doorway, trying so hard to look calm that it made him seem more rattled.

“You’re both awake,” he said.

“You knew she could do that?” I asked.

“No.” The answer came too fast.

His eyes flicked to Mio, then to the room, as if he were recalling a procedure he’d rather not have to explain here. The visibility rule still applied: anyone who crossed into the doorway could see her. The private room had acquired a witness range.

“This isn’t a school presentation,” Nico said. “And the projection isn’t stable.”

Mio stopped pacing. She took the side of the room where we would have to keep existing around each other.

“It’s a side effect,” Nico said, “not proof that she’s a person.”

The words came out precise. Too precise.

Mio’s expression tightened. She didn’t look away.

“Other systems may be able to register her now,” Nico continued. “Cameras. Biometrics. Recognition filters. Maybe people.”

The problem had outgrown the room. What had been private embarrassment was now a risk that could spread through every system watching us.

Nico looked at me. “Bad enough for you?”
